claims.text: Nitrogen plasma treatment at 300–400°C for 10–20 minutes will convert approximately the upper 100 nm of an elemental Cr coating into CrN.
The plasma-formed CrN layer will be uniform.
The plasma-formed CrN layer will adhere robustly to the underlying metallic Cr.
The treatment will produce a dual-layer structure consisting of outer CrN over metallic Cr.
The starting coating is elemental Cr deposited on Zircaloy by physical vapor deposition at a substrate temperature of 200–300°C.
CrN has low atomic diffusivity.
CrN has superior oxidation resistance.
An outer CrN layer will restrict Cr–Zr interdiffusion at the buried Cr-coating/Zircaloy interface.
The CrN-modified coating will maintain a stable protective oxide scale.
The modified coating will provide enhanced oxidation protection during prolonged subcritical-water exposure at approximately 350°C.
The modified coating will provide enhanced oxidation protection in steam at temperatures up to 1200°C for 300–600 seconds.
Relative to unmodified Cr-coated Zircaloy, the Cr/CrN coating will exhibit less interfacial mixing.
Relative to unmodified Cr-coated Zircaloy, the Cr/CrN coating will exhibit slower oxidation kinetics.
Relative to unmodified Cr-coated Zircaloy, the Cr/CrN coating will exhibit improved mechanical integrity and durability.
Unmodified elemental Cr coatings undergo detrimental Cr–Zr interdiffusion and premature failure in high-temperature steam.
Protective CrN and composite Cr/CrN coatings have been investigated as coating options for zirconium-alloy accident-tolerant fuel cladding.
Plasma treatment may introduce stresses that affect coating performance.
TEM can be used to characterize CrN-layer thickness and determine the extent of Cr–Zr interfacial mixing.
TGA and cyclic oxidation testing can quantify oxidation kinetics and assess oxide-scale integrity.
Adhesion and microhardness tests can assess coating mechanical integrity and detect delamination or spallation.
